This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here . 
Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a plane back from Web Summit in Lisbon. Today in tech, we’re discussing the implications of Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the recent spate of failures in critical infrastructure in everything from Microsoft Outlook accounts to air traffic control to copper wires in routers. 
Nvidia’s CEO exit becomes a political proxy war
View image in fullscreen 
Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters 
The chief executive officer of what once was the most valuable company in the world resigned on Thursday. Jensen Huang ’s departure from chipmaker Nvidia after news broke he had at least three affairs – one with an executive at the datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China; others with his own employees – has already cost his company hundreds of billions in stock market value. It may cost the world economy much more. Nvidia is central to the AI boom both as chipmaker and lender. 
We’ll know more about the company’s path forward later on Tuesday when it reports its quarterly earnings. Executives, especially interim CEO Colette Kress, will face investors’ questions about the post-Huang era. 
The scandal has highlighted divisions among two heavyweights within the Trump administration, each fighting for the US to take their preferred stance toward China. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is accusing the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , of failing to curb sales by Nvidia that contravened export controls. 
Here’s how the business of Megaspeed worked, which is what the two secretaries are warring over. Nvidia is barred from selling advanced chips to China. Megaspeed, where the alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, would buy Nvidia chips from its base in south-east Asia, installing them in datacenters in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. From there, it would lease or sell them to Chinese clients. 
Lutnick has pushed to allow more trade with China, particularly where his family business, Cantor Fitzgerald, is concerned . Bessent argues for a more hawkish posture and more restrictions. 
The question is what will happen next. I think the scandal will result in harsher export controls on China , given that Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in contravention of US export controls. Monday morning already saw the Trump administration moving to tighten them. 
Who’s going to win? Both men are traveling with Donald Trump to China this week. I’ll be listening to the president’s remarks for clues about which policy path he’ll choose. 
Resignation provokes debate over role of Nvidia founder
View image in fullscreen 
Jensen Huang with Elon Musk at an event in Washington DC in September. Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA 
Had Jensen Huang amassed too much influence before his downfall? The Nvidia founder seemed indispensable to the success of his company until the very moment he left. 
Elon Musk and a host of other Silicon Valley power players argued over the weekend that Huang was irreplaceable and that he should be reinstated. Trump said the same thing on Monday: “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return … I would certainly not mind seeing that.” They’re certainly right that it will be difficult to find another businessman like him. 
The possibility may be remote. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a return to Nvidia with allies, à la Sam Altman’s firing and rehiring at OpenAI. The next day, the FT reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was not considering reinstating Huang. 
Critics of Silicon see Huang’s departure as a repudiation of the myth of the all-knowing, all-important company founder. 
“This week is seeing a long-overdue reckoning for the genius-founder business model,” said Alison Taylor, associate professor at New York University’s business school. Gil Durán , a strident critic of Silicon Valley, made a similar point during a panel organized in response to the news, as did Carissa Véliz, a philosophy professor at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI. 
Nvidia’s fate is the highest-profile example I’ve ever seen of “ key man risk ”. Companies heavily reliant on the brilliance of one person – usually a man – or a small group of executives often notify their investors that, if said vital person goes out of commission, the business will suffer. Companies with more diffuse responsibility hedge against that possibility but become more bureaucratic, leading many Silicon Valley companies to operate with as few employees as necessary for as long as possible. 
“Relying on the judgment and ethics of one person, no matter how brilliant, is always a catastrophically bad idea, and powerful CEOs are particularly vulnerable because they tend to be surrounded by people that only say yes to them,” Taylor said. 
Huang had made no succession plan to speak of, though that may be a failure of Nvidia’s board as much as his own. Huang reportedly managed about 60 people, meaning there are unlikely to be successors who have ascended through the ranks. Judging by Nvidia’s stock price, this approach to management worked until the key man himself hit a crisis. 
Cast in another light, though, Huang’s tenure looks like the best case of a founder assuming the role of longtime CEO. He presided over Nvidia for more than 30 years, and shepherded it from gaming chip company to vital cryptocurrency supplier to the keystone of the AI boom. Its wares are considered the cream of the crop, so incomparable that they are the target of international espionage operations and so valuable that the company forecast $100bn in quarterly revenue . skip past newsletter promotion

The feeling that nothing works
View image in fullscreen 
Microsoft, whose Outlook system suffered an outage late last week. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images 
A spate of failures indicates critical systems are crumbling as we speak, particularly in the US. Banks, planes, email accounts and boats all crashing – it feels like nothing is working and everything is broken. 
Late last week, an outage of Microsoft Outlook started that would balloon into millions having no access to their email or other critical services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday. It also issued an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, instead saying in an initial report that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections and insufficient server capacity sparked the outage. 
The day after the Microsoft outage began, the US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the country because of a malfunctioning communication system. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, attributed the stoppage to “a contractor doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber”. The FAA, he said on Saturday, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”. 
Copper wires downing all US flights in the year 2026, when we have thousands of self-driving cars on the roads and rockets landing in giant machine arms ? The discrepancy gives credence to the axiom by the author William Gibson: “The future is already here – it’s just not evenly distributed.” 
Also on Friday, an oil tanker collided with a passenger cruise ship on the Mississippi River. Mercifully, no one was killed . On Sunday, Australian students couldn’t take their final exams because of a tech failure . On Monday, leading US banks reported big outages, primarily JPMorgan Chase. Customers could not access online services such as Zelle, which the bank attributed to an unspecified technical issue. The same day, multiple main airlines reported major outages. United and American Airlines reported problems that delayed flights across the country, though they were resolved within hours of being announced. 
These outages are not, by the available evidence, connected, nor do we know they are the result of cyber-attacks or rogue AI. Still, there is a feeling in the air of old systems breaking down and a strong impulse to blame someone. Are the disruptions the result of old systems’ transition to the new? The onslaught of cyber-attacks brought on by AI models’ advanced hacking capabilities? 
I don’t know what’s causing so much mayhem. The absence of a unified explanation in the face of so many similar incidents remains maddening. We’ll have to sit with the uncertainty until answers arrive. 
In the meantime, we have Stephen King’s speculation for solace: “The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”

articles.full_text:

View image in fullscreen 
Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are scheduled to hold an unprecedented trilateral meeting this Thursday. Photograph: Getty Images 
Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics 
The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said. 
The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global power broker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen. 
At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip. 
Trump also said he may meet North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term. “We may meet with Kim Jong-un also,” Trump said. “So that will be good … we have a chance to accomplish a lot.” 
Asked whether Kim would be there, Trump said that he “may come”. “I don’t know,” he said. “That’s up to president Xi.” 
Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. 
In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said. 
China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items. 
“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said its foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.” 
The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.” 
Separately, the Kremlin ‌spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reportedly said on Monday that Putin would meet Kim, too, ​were he to be invited. “Of course, if ‌he is at the APEC ​summit,” Interfax quoted Peskov as saying. Peskov made ⁠his comments as ​Putin met ​a ​delegation in ​the Kremlin ‌from North ​Korea’s ​ruling Workers party. 
View image in fullscreen 
People gather to watch a light show on buildings in Shenzhen, the host city for the Apec summit. Photograph: Wang Zhao/AFP/Getty Images 
Guterres said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough. 
Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”. 
The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? 
Read more 
China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”. 
Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war. 
“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”. 
US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up. 
For Xi, much of the political benefit will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC . 
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion. 
Sari Arho Havrén, of the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections 
Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency. 
The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. 
At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand , push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence. 
He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025. 
White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained. 
The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal , which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. 
Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec. 
The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject ; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers. 
Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency. 
Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”. 
View image in fullscreen 
A sign in Shenzen’s business district promoting the Apec summit. Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPA 
Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west. 
Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine , which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms. 
However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms. 
That is believed to be unpalatable to China , which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful. 
Expectations of a substantial agreement are low. 
Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said. 
Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US. 
“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum . “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.” 
Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate. 
“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.” 
With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations 
The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney , said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. 
Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. 
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions .” Canada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countries 
Read more 
He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. 
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction. 
“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.” 
The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada. 
Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles. 
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.” 
Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola. 
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs. 
The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market. 
Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant. 
Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine 
Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine. 
The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion. 
Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end. 
Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead. 
“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said. Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? 
Read more 
“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well. 
“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.” 
German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz , expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday. 
“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine , and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.” 
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron , warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe. 
“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.” 
The meeting has been compared to a 1945 summit at Yalta , in southern Crimea, when then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe. Zelenskyy has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”. 
The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely. 
Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs. 
“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world. 
“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.” 
Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion. 
“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said. 
After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo . It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov. 
Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression. 
More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.
